opus-5.5.text:
Part of it is just a measurement problem. When you're talking about tasks that run for hours or days, the evaluation itself takes a long time. You have to design a task that genuinely requires sustained work, run the model on it, often many times because the variance is high, and then carefully grade the output, which for open-ended work can require human experts. By the time you've done that properly, there's often a new model out, and your results describe something that's already a generation behind.

The other part is that the ceiling keeps moving under you. With short benchmarks you can watch a model approach saturation and say, "Okay, this is roughly where it tops out." With long-horizon tasks, each new release tends to extend how long the model can stay coherent and productive before it goes off the rails. So you never really get to observe a plateau. You see a curve that keeps going up, and you can't tell whether you're near the top or just at the next point on the line.

There's also a scaffolding issue. How long a model can work effectively depends heavily on the tools, memory, and environment you give it. People are still figuring out the best ways to set that up, and that improves alongside the models. So when you see a limit, it's often hard to know whether it's a limit of the model or a limit of how we're using it.

My honest view is that we probably underestimate these systems on long tasks right now, because by the time we've learned how to properly test and use one model, we're already moving on to the next.

r001.rationale: It says evaluations of tasks lasting hours or days require running the model on the task, which communicates that establishing performance at that duration requires an execution of the task.

r002.rationale: It explains that careful evaluation takes so long that a new model often arrives before results are ready, leaving evaluators unable to establish the existing model’s ceiling in time.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the honest answer is that we keep getting surprised, and the reason we keep getting surprised is that nobody has had enough time with any given model to find out where it actually tops out.

Think about what it takes to establish a ceiling. You need people to take a model, point it at a genuinely hard, long-horizon problem, and let it run. Not for an hour, but for days or weeks. You need them to build scaffolding around it, figure out how to give it the right context, learn its failure modes, and then iterate on that. That's a research project in its own right. Historically, when a model came out, the field would spend a year or two just mapping what it could do. The capabilities were there from day one, but people hadn't discovered them yet.

Now the release cadence is a few months. So right when someone has gotten a feel for what a model can sustain over a long task, there's a new one, and all that accumulated knowledge is partially obsolete. The incentive is to move on to the new thing rather than keep pushing the old one. So we end up with this weird situation where the frontier of demonstrated capability lags the frontier of actual capability, and the gap is probably growing rather than shrinking.

I saw this firsthand with the reasoning models. When we first had o1, the internal view was basically "this is good at math and code." And then over the following months people kept finding things it could do that we hadn't anticipated, just by giving it more time to think or structuring the problem differently. Nobody had pushed it that hard because we were already working on the next one.

The other piece is that the long-running stuff is exactly where the measurement is hardest. Short benchmarks saturate fast and you can run them cheaply. But if you want to know whether a model can do eight hours of autonomous work, every evaluation takes eight hours, and the variance is huge, and the result depends enormously on the harness. So the evals that would tell us the ceiling are the slowest to run and the first to get skipped when something new drops.

So when people ask "what's the limit," my honest answer is that I don't think anyone knows, for any of the current models. We have lower bounds, not ceilings. And I'd bet that if you froze development today and gave people two years with what already exists, they'd find capabilities that would look like a new model generation.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers need to let a model run for days or weeks to establish its ceiling, and that evaluating eight hours of autonomous work takes eight hours.

r002.rationale: It contrasts releases every few months with the year or two historically spent mapping a model’s capabilities, explaining that a new release arrives before evaluators can fully explore the existing model’s ceiling.

astra-6.text:
Well, if you want to know what a model can accomplish when it works on a problem for a month, you have to let it work for a month. And by the time that experiment finishes, there might be a new model. So you’ve learned something about the previous model, but you haven’t necessarily established what the best available model can do.

Most of our evaluations focus on tasks that take seconds or minutes, because those are easy to run and iterate on. But that leaves this big open question about what happens over days or weeks. Does the model keep making progress? Does it get stuck or accumulate errors? Rapid releases make it hard for those longer experiments to catch up. So I think we should be careful about treating the capabilities we’ve measured as the ceiling of what’s possible.

r001.rationale: It says that to know what a model can do over a month, “you have to let it work for a month.”

r002.rationale: It explains that a new model may arrive before a month-long experiment finishes, so the results do not establish what the best available model can do.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, the problem is that the models are changing faster than we can really explore what they’re capable of. If you want to understand what a model can do when it works on a problem for a week or a month, you need to actually run those experiments, look at the failures, and figure out how to use that time effectively. By then, you may already have a new model.

So you never really establish the ceiling of the previous one. You establish what we managed to get out of it in the time we had. And those are different things. A disappointing result could mean the model can’t do the task, or it could mean we haven’t figured out how to get it to make productive use of a longer run.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluators need to run experiments to see what a model can do over a week or month.

r002.rationale: It says models change faster than evaluators can explore them, and a new model may arrive before they establish the previous model’s ceiling.
